# Sañjīvajātaka (Ja 150)

**ID:** Ja 150
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Suttas-Late-1
**Title (Pali):** Sañjīvajātaka
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul0.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Sañjīvajātaka* (Ja 150) is the concluding story of the *Kakaṇṭakavagga* in the *Ekanipāta* of the Pali Jātaka collection [Fausböll 1877]. Its frame story (*paccuppannavatthu*) is set at the Bamboo Grove in Rājagaha, delivered concerning King Ajātasattu's infatuation with the schismatic Devadatta, his funding of the monastery at Gayāsīsa, and his subsequent patricide [Juan Wu 2012]. Scholars note that the story of the present represents an adaptation of the frame story of the *Sāmaññaphalasutta* (DN 2), integrating the Vinaya's Devadatta episode with Ajātasattu's remorse and quest for reconciliation with the Buddha [Juan Wu 2012; Lang Chen 2015; Radich 2011].

In the story of the past (*atītavatthu*), the Bodhisatta was a world-renowned brahmin teacher whose pupil, Sañjīva, learned a charm capable of reviving the dead, though he was never taught the counter-charm [UNDV 2009; Fausböll 1877]. Filled with arrogance, the youth used the spell to revive a dead tiger in the forest, which promptly mauled and killed him [UNDV 2009]. The Bodhisatta uttered the moral verse cautioning against befriending or exalting the wicked [Fausböll 1877]. In the identification of the birth (*samodhāna*), the Buddha explains that the foolish pupil who revived the tiger was Ajātasattu in a past life, while the teacher was the Bodhisatta [Fausböll 1877].
